title: THE EXPLAINED FUTURE
sub: An essay in four moves, answered by the archive. The narration is a draft: every line can be rewritten by what comes back.

lines.text: In the years after the war, companies and governments made thousands of films to explain the future to the people who would have to live in it.
The engineers believed that if every task could be measured, every life could be improved.
Kitchens were redesigned so that a woman would take fewer steps between the stove and the sink.
But the cameras kept recording things their makers had not meant to show.
In the factories, men stood beside machines that no longer needed them.
Then the television arrived in the living room, and promised to bring the whole world inside.
What came inside was a picture of the world that someone else had already arranged.
At the same time, in committee rooms, other men were deciding how much the future would cost.
They spoke a new language of budgets and forecasts, in which no one person was ever responsible.
And the people in the films began to say things that did not fit the plan.
In the schools, children practised air-raid drills, crouching under their desks.
Their parents drove, flew and built faster than any generation before them, toward a place nobody could describe.
The future had been explained to them. Nobody had asked them what they wanted.
